entry.reasons: The entry accurately reflects the essential knowledge statements 3.2.A.3.ii and 3.2.A.3.iv from the AP Physics C: Mechanics CED Unit 3. The topic code is correct, and the content is directly required by the course framework.

The body closely tracks Topic 3.2 essential knowledge. CED 3.2.A.3.ii states that only the force component parallel to the displacement of its point of application changes the system’s total energy. CED 3.2.A.3.iv states that a component perpendicular to the displacement of the system’s center of mass can change the direction of motion without changing kinetic energy. Both statements are required in Topic 3.2, and no caution is needed.

a_factual: The first sentence matches essential knowledge 3.2.A.3.ii: "Only the component of the force exerted on a system that is parallel to the displacement of the point of application of the force will change the system's total energy." The second sentence matches 3.2.A.3.iv: "The component of the force exerted on a system perpendicular to the direction of the displacement of the system's center of mass can change the direction of the system's motion without changing the system's kinetic energy." No symbols or formulas are involved. b_topic_codes: Both cited statements sit under Topic 3.2 (Work), and this is the first unit/topic where the CED requires them, so owner_topic_code 3.2 and topic_codes [3.2] are correct. c_ced_required: 3.2.A.3.ii and 3.2.A.3.iv are essential-knowledge statements under learning objective 3.2.A (describe the work done by a given force), so the CED requires students to apply this. d_caution: The entry paraphrases the CED very closely and keeps the point-earning wording (parallel to the displacement of the point of application; perpendicular to the displacement of the center of mass). No caution is needed, and caution is null, which is correct.

The entry accurately represents Essential Knowledge 3.2.A.4.iii from the CED, which states: 'The energy dissipated by friction is typically equated to the force of friction times the length of the path over which the force is exerted.' The caution correctly highlights the distinction between path length and net displacement, which is a common point of confusion.

Topic 3.2, essential knowledge 3.2.A.4.iii states: “The energy dissipated by friction is typically equated to the force of friction times the length of the path over which the force is exerted.” The formula and caution use path length rather than net displacement, consistent with that statement.

a_factual: The CED states the relation as an approximation: 3.2.A.4.iii reads "The energy dissipated by friction is typically equated to the force of friction times the length of the path over which the force is exerted." The entry's E_dissipated ≈ F_f s, with s defined as path length, matches that wording and its 'typically' approximation. b_topic_codes: The statement sits under LO 3.2.A in Topic 3.2 (Work), the only topic that uses it, so owner_topic_code and topic_codes ['3.2'] are correct. c_ced_required: 3.2.A.4.iii is an essential-knowledge statement under LO 3.2.A ("Describe the work done on an object or system by a given force or collection of forces"), so students are required to apply it. d_caution: The CED phrases the point as 'typically equated to ... the length of the path', not as an exact equality. The entry's ≈ and its caution (path length, not net displacement) capture that wording and the path-vs-displacement distinction, so the caution is present and correct.

The entry accurately represents the work-energy theorem as defined in EK 3.2.A.4. The caution correctly notes the conditions for variable vs. constant forces as described in EK 3.2.A.3 and 3.2.A.3.iii.

Topic 3.2.A.4 states that “the change in an object’s kinetic energy is equal to the sum of the work (net work) being done by all forces exerted on the object,” supporting ΔK = ΣᵢWᵢ. The caution correctly specifies all forces and reflects 3.2.A.3’s variable-force treatment and 3.2.A.3.iii’s constant-parallel-component condition.

a_factual: CED 3.2.A.4 states 'the change in an object's kinetic energy is equal to the sum of the work (net work) being done by all forces exerted on the object,' which matches ΔK = Σ W_i. The symbols and the summation over forces are correct. b_topic_codes: The theorem first appears in topic 3.2 (3.2.A.4). Topic 3.1 introduces only K = ½mv² and topic 3.3 introduces potential energy, so owner_topic_code 3.2 is correct, and topic_codes ['3.2'] is the only unit topic that states it. c_ced_required: Learning objective 3.2.A ('Describe the work done on an object or system by a given force or collection of forces') and essential knowledge 3.2.A.4 explicitly require students to know and apply the work–energy theorem. d_caution: The CED wording is 'sum of the work (net work) being done by all forces,' while the entry uses symbolic ΔK = Σ W_i, so a caution is needed. The caution says 'The sum is the net work done by all forces exerted on the object (3.2.A.4),' which matches the CED. Its second sentence correctly reflects 3.2.A.3: for a variable force, W_i is the path integral, and the force × displacement form applies when the parallel component is constant (3.2.A.3.iii). The caution is accurate and present.
